summary:
Kansas visitors are subject to Kansas law as well as to the United States federal framework, which the national profile carries. Kansas Senate Bill 244 was enacted on 26 February 2026 through a legislative override of Governor Laura Kelly's veto and took effect immediately.

SB 244 confines trans people to sex-segregated facilities matching sex assigned at birth. The Human Rights Campaign records that the restriction covers public buildings including schools, universities, airports and government offices. The ACLU of Kansas states that the law creates new civil and criminal penalties, and the statute sets fines of up to $1,000 for using a gender-segregated facility in a publicly owned building when the user's gender does not match sex assigned at birth. It also authorises any private individual to sue for at least $1,000 over a bathroom or locker-room encounter with a trans person, a private-enforcement provision that has no parallel in neighbouring jurisdictions.

A legal-risk assessment published on 20 February 2026 moved Kansas from its "Worst Laws" tier to "Do Not Travel", the first state added to that tier in a year. The reclassification follows the private-suit provision and the exposure it creates for a trans person moving through the state, including interstate transit through Kansas airports and government buildings.

Identity documents are the second exposure. SB 244 bars trans people from updating a driver's licence or state ID and invalidates existing licences whose gender marker is inconsistent with sex assigned at birth. Documents must be reissued at the holder's expense with no grace period, and holders receive surrender letters warning of additional penalties for driving without a valid credential. The ACLU of Kansas reports that the Department of Revenue has been mailing written notice and that many holders have already been told their licence is now invalid.

Two trans men filed Doe v. State of Kansas within days of SB 244's enactment, represented by the ACLU of Kansas and Ballard Spahr in Douglas County District Court, citing fear of violence under the bathroom-restriction and ID-invalidation provisions. The challenge was still pending as of the sources' reporting, so the operative position of the law should be checked before travel.

The document restrictions follow three years of litigation. Senate Bill 180, enacted in April 2023 over Governor Kelly's veto, defined biological sex in state law and barred agencies from recognising genders beyond sex assigned at birth; the attorney general then directed that new or updated driver's licences and birth certificates reflect only sex assigned at birth. A temporary restraining order blocked gender-marker changes, the Kansas Court of Appeals reversed unanimously on 13 June 2025 for lack of evidence of irreparable harm to law-enforcement identification, and the Kansas Supreme Court declined an appeal in October 2025, allowing the Department of Revenue to continue processing changes until SB 244 ended them.

Discrimination protections survive at state level. Kansas law has prohibited discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations since 2020, following Bostock v. Clayton County and Kansas Human Rights Commission action in August 2020 covering businesses with four or more employees. The state hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by sexual orientation but does not cover gender identity, so a bias-motivated assault against a trans person carries no state-level enhancement.

Gender-affirming care for minors under 18 has been banned since Senate Bill 63 was overridden on 18 February 2025. In May 2026 State District Judge Carl Folsom III granted a temporary injunction blocking enforcement in an ACLU-backed parental lawsuit, so the ban is not being enforced while that case proceeds.

Marriage is not restricted by gender. Same-sex marriage became available after U.S. District Judge Daniel D. Crabtree ruled the state ban unconstitutional on 4 November 2014, effective 12 November 2014, and became fully legal under Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015, replacing the prior statutory and constitutional bans on same-sex marriage and other unions. A trans visitor's marriage is recognised on the same terms.
tangentialFactors:
Rights groups describe SB 244 as a template for other state legislatures, and further Kansas bills targeting trans people were reported pending as of early 2026, so the legal environment is moving rather than settled.

The legislative trajectory runs from symbolic restriction to enforceable restriction. SB 180 in 2023 prohibited entering sex-segregated bathrooms, crisis shelters, prisons and other biology, safety or privacy accommodations not matching sex assigned at birth, but carried no enforcement mechanism; SB 244 added fines, criminal exposure and the private-suit provision to the same conduct. Earlier attempts met vetoes that were overridden: the school sports ban was vetoed in 2021, 2022 and March 2023 before taking effect on 1 July 2023, and the minors' care ban survived a failed override by two votes in April 2024 before passing in February 2025.

Local and state directions have diverged before. Roeland Park banned conversion therapy on minors in June 2020, Lawrence in April 2021 and Prairie Village in October 2021, while voters in Salina and Hutchinson repealed local non-discrimination ordinances on 6 November 2012 and state-level executive orders on the subject were rescinded in 2015 and reissued in 2019.

In March 2024 the Legislature passed a law defining content containing "acts of homosexuality" as harmful to minors alongside pornography and requiring government ID-based age verification to access such material, an access restriction that also affects how adults reach information online.

Kansas's sodomy statute has never been repealed. Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been unenforceable since Lawrence v. Texas in 2003 rendered it so, but the legislature left its same-sex-only provisions on the books carrying historic penalties of six months in jail and a $1,000 fine, and State v. Limon invalidated the harsher Romeo-and-Juliet sentences applied to same-sex parties.
localsOnly:
Residents must surrender non-compliant licences and pay for reissue, with no grace period; the surrender letters warn of additional penalties for driving without a valid credential, and the Department of Revenue has been issuing written notice directly to holders.

Transgender athletes have been barred from female school sports teams since the ban took effect on 1 July 2023. As of February 2023 the Kansas State High School Activities Association left eligibility decisions case-by-case to individual schools, a practice the sources do not update beyond that date.

Gender-affirming care for minors is banned under Senate Bill 63, overridden on 18 February 2025 after Governor Kelly's veto, and enforcement is currently blocked by the temporary injunction granted by State District Judge Carl Folsom III in May 2026 in an ACLU-backed parental lawsuit. Governor Kelly had vetoed the earlier Senate Bill 233 on 12 April 2024 and the override failed by two votes.

Employment, housing and public accommodations discrimination on the basis of gender identity has been prohibited since 2020 through Bostock v. Clayton County and Kansas Human Rights Commission enforcement, reaching businesses with four or more employees, supplemented by city ordinances.

Adoption and assisted reproduction are open to same-sex couples: married same-sex couples may adopt, lesbian couples may access in vitro fertilisation with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognised only if married, and the state permits gestational and traditional surrogacy on equal terms for same-sex and different-sex couples. Adoption agencies may refuse placements that violate their religious or moral convictions, and under In the Matter of Adoption of I.M. (November 2012) and Frazier v. Goudschaal (22 February 2013) unmarried non-biological partners obtain rights only in limited best-interest circumstances.

In 2022 a Geary County middle-school teacher obtained a partial federal preliminary injunction allowing her to use students' non-preferred names and to out students to parents, despite a school preferred-name requirement.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports how many private suits have been filed under the SB 244 bounty provision, or how the facility penalties have been charged in practice. Enforcement volume is unresolved.

The inventory contains no documented incident of violence against a trans person in Kansas with a date and outcome, so the state's violence risk rests on the statutory exposure and on the plaintiffs' stated fear of violence in Doe v. State of Kansas rather than on incident data.

Whether SB 244's facility and document provisions face legal challenge beyond Doe v. State of Kansas is not sourced, and the outcome of that case is not reported. The assessment should be re-checked against the current court position before travel.

The interaction between an invalidated Kansas licence and federal transport or entry document checks is not addressed by any source here; that layer belongs to the national record.

The Kansas State High School Activities Association's case-by-case practice is dated February 2023 and may since have changed. The status of the further bills reported pending in early 2026 is likewise unresolved.
